lookForward.fits: Marathon weekend in Berlin: Saturday 26 September 2026 the Generali 5K from Potsdamer Platz and the inline-skating marathon, Sunday 27 September the marathon from 8:30; all inside the city.
lookForward.headline: Marathon weekend: from Saturday the streets belong to the runners
lookForward.line: Saturday brings a 5-kilometre run over the last stretch of the course from Potsdamer Platz, then the inline-skating marathon. Sunday from 8:30, the marathon itself: 55,000 runners, finishing at the Brandenburg Gate. Pick a spot on the route and clap.

goodThing.fits: Autumn is when Berliners refill their bottles from the tap after a hot summer; a local fact worth being proud of.
goodThing.headline: Berlin's tap water comes straight from the ground
goodThing.line: Pumped from under the city, cleaned with air and sand, no chlorine added. Checked at more than 3,300 points.
more: Berlin sits on sand. Under the city, the two broad valleys carved by ice-age meltwater, the Spree and Havel valleys, are full of groundwater held in sand and gravel. The waterworks pump from about 650 wells there, and much of what they pump is river water that seeped down through the sandy banks over weeks and months, filtered on the way.

At the works the water is aerated, which turns dissolved iron and manganese into particles, and then run through sand filters that catch them. That is the whole treatment. No chlorine, no fluoride, nothing added, because nothing needs to be.

The price of this is hardness: Berlin water carries a lot of lime, which is why kettles fur up. It is also why it tastes of something. The company tests it at more than 3,300 points, from the wells to the pipes to taps in ordinary flats, and publishes the results by district.
So the bottle in the fridge is a habit, not a need. The tap is fine. The tap is, by most measures, better.

onThisDay.headline: West Berlin opened its new opera house
onThisDay.line: The Deutsche Oper on Bismarckstraße, six weeks after the Wall went up. The first night was Mozart's Don Giovanni.
more: West Berlin had lost its opera house twice: bombed in 1943, rebuilt, and then cut off from the two other houses on the eastern side when the Wall went up on 13 August 1961. Six weeks later, on 24 September, the new Deutsche Oper on Bismarckstraße opened, a long concrete block by the architect Fritz Bornemann that looks like nothing much from the street and holds nearly 1,900 people inside.

Ferenc Fricsay conducted Don Giovanni on the first night, with Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau in the title role. The house took a new name for the occasion: it had been the Städtische Oper, the municipal opera; from that night it was the Deutsche Oper Berlin, a claim to be the opera of the Germans, at a time when the city was newly divided.

Today Berlin has three opera houses again, more than any other city, and the one on Bismarckstraße is the biggest. The U-Bahn station outside is named after it. Tickets for the back rows cost about what a cinema does.

funFact.fits: A Berlin fact for a Berlin reader; the Spree and Havel are at their calmest in early autumn.
funFact.statement: Berlin has more bridges than Venice.
funFact.reveal: Around a thousand, against Venice's four hundred. Many of Berlin's cross railways and roads rather than water, but they count.

source.name: t-online: Warum Berlin mehr Brücken als Venedig hat

more: The bridge count depends on who is counting. Berlin’s statistics office says about 970. The city’s senate has said more than 1,100. Venice, in its historic centre, has around 400. The difference is what counts as a bridge.

Berlin counts every crossing that belongs to the city: bridges over the Spree and the Havel and the canals, but also bridges over railway lines, over motorways, over other roads. Most of them are not pretty and nobody photographs them. Venice’s bridges are almost all over water, and most of them are photographed daily.

Still, the water is real. Berlin has more than 180 kilometres of navigable waterways inside the city limits, and the Oberbaumbrücke, the Glienicke Bridge and the little bridges of the Spreewald quarter are as good as any. The claim is technically true. It is also a very Berlin thing to say.

calmRead.fits: A Berlin place for a bright Thursday evening in late September: Tempelhofer Feld, sunset on the runway.
calmRead.title: The airport where kites fly now
calmRead.teaser: A field the size of a district lies in the middle of Berlin. Nobody may build on it.
paragraphs: Take the U6 to Paradestraße this evening and walk through the gate. In front of you is something you do not expect in a city: more than 300 hectares of grass and concrete, two runways, no house, no tree in the way. Planes landed here until 2008. Since May 2010 Tempelhofer Feld has been a park, one of the largest open spaces inside any city in the world.

The airport itself is history: the huge building along the edge was once among the largest in the world, and in 1948 and 1949, during the Berlin Blockade, a plane carrying coal and flour landed here every few minutes. Berliners called them raisin bombers. The field remembers that, but it lives differently now.

In 2014 the city wanted to build along the edges. Berliners voted, and almost two thirds said no. Since then a law protects the field: no houses, no roads. Skylarks nest in the meadow in the middle, which is why it is fenced off in spring. On the runways there are skaters, cyclists and children with pinwheels, and anyone with a kite has the best wind in the city.

In late September the sun sets shortly after seven, and on the field you see it from beginning to end, because nothing stands in the way. Bring a blanket and something to drink, sit down on the runway and look west. By half past seven it is over, and the whole city has become an hour quieter.

joke.fits: Tempelhofer Feld, from today’s calm read.
joke.setup: Why don’t planes land at Tempelhof any more?
joke.punchline: Too many kites on the approach.

riddle.fits: Tempelhofer Feld, from today’s calm read.
riddle.riddle: I have two runways and no planes, I am bigger than 400 football pitches, and in the evening the whole sky is mine. What am I?
